title: The Connection Approval Gap: Why a Completed Solar Job Isn't a Paid One Yet
linkedin:
For a solar and battery installer, the job looks finished the day the panels go up and the system switches on.

Commercially, it isn't.

On most residential contracts, the final payment doesn't release until the distribution network service provider approves the new connection. That approval sits completely outside the installer's control, and it can take anywhere from a few days to several weeks.

Spring widens the gap. Bookings lift as households and small businesses get ahead of summer bills, and battery storage has become a bigger part of the average job. Batteries carry a higher unit cost than panels and inverters alone, so a growing attachment rate is good for revenue and also means more cash sitting in each individual job for longer.

The installer has already paid for materials and labour on a job that is, by every practical measure, finished. The cash to cover that outlay is still sitting in a network operator's approval queue, not in the business's account.

The number worth tracking isn't total revenue booked for the month. It's how much cash is currently committed across every job sitting between completion and connection approval, set against what's actually due to suppliers and staff in that same window.

Most job management systems already hold this data. Few installation businesses have turned it into a rolling cash picture rather than a job by job list.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
